task_row_model.query: In a mixed-methods educational intervention trial with several planned and many exploratory subgroup analyses, what principled approaches can I use to correct for multiple comparisons across subgroup tests while preserving statistical power? Summarize practical frequentist and Bayesian options, how to prioritize tests, and the trade-offs involved.

documents.content: Standard multiplicity corrections are often invoked when multiple hypothesis tests are performed. Bonferroni and Holm procedures control the family-wise error rate by adjusting p-value thresholds based on the number of tests; Bonferroni divides alpha by the count of tests, while Holm is stepwise and uniformly more powerful. False discovery rate (FDR) methods such as Benjamini–Hochberg control expected proportion of false positives and are often used when many comparisons are exploratory. Permutation-based maxT procedures account for correlation among tests and can be less conservative than Bonferroni in high-correlation settings.

Ethical oversight in educational research requires attention to informed consent, privacy, and equitable treatment of participants. Institutional review boards assess risk–benefit balance and data handling plans. When interventions are delivered at the classroom or school level investigators should justify cluster-level consent procedures, explain how vulnerable populations are protected, and outline plans for disseminating results. Transparency about preregistration and reporting of null or negative findings helps protect participant trust and reduces publication bias in the field.

A practical strategy blends pre-specification, hierarchical testing, and shrinkage-based modeling. Pre-specify a small set of primary subgroup analyses and treat others as exploratory. For frequentist control, use gatekeeping or hierarchical testing to preserve alpha for primary hypotheses and apply Holm or stepdown procedures within families; permutation-based maxT can exploit correlation to maintain power. For exploratory sets, apply FDR procedures rather than strict FWER control. Bayesian hierarchical models provide partial pooling across subgroups, shrinking extreme estimates and effectively addressing multiplicity while yielding probabilistic statements; trade-offs include interpretability and sensitivity to priors. Emphasize interaction tests over separate within-subgroup tests and report which comparisons were pre-specified.

Bayesian hierarchical modeling offers a coherent way to handle many subgroup estimates by modeling subgroup effects as draws from a common distribution. Partial pooling reduces variance of noisy subgroup estimates and mitigates apparent large effects due to multiple comparisons. Posterior summaries (credible intervals, posterior probabilities of direction) can be reported for each subgroup, and shrinkage reduces the need for multiplicity-adjusting p-value corrections. Limitations include dependence on prior choices, potential skepticism from audiences accustomed to p-values, and complexity of model specification and checking.

Sample size calculation for cluster randomized trials requires accounting for intracluster correlation (ICC). Effective sample size is reduced by the design effect (1 + (m-1)ICC) where m is cluster size. Power formulas differ from individually randomized designs and require assumptions about between-cluster variance and expected effect size. When planning, investigators should consider number of clusters as more influential on power than cluster size, sensitivity analyses for ICC values, and potential loss to follow-up at cluster and individual levels. Adjustments for multiple outcomes may further inflate required sample size.
